references.text: Isaiah encourages not to fear human mockery and scorn for the sake of righteousness, which reflects Jesus' words about being blessed when people mock and persecute you.

Isaiah speaks of those who hate and cast out their brothers for the Lord's name's sake, but the Lord will show Himself as a joy to them—a parallel to being cast out and hated for the Son of Man's sake.

Matthew's version of the beatitude about persecution: 'Blessed are you when they mock and persecute you and falsely say all kinds of evil against you on my account.' This is the closest parallel to Luke 6:22.
Jesus says that disciples will be hated by all for his name's sake, which reflects the theme of being hated by people for the Son of Man's sake.
Jesus says that the world hates disciples because it hated him first, and that they are not of the world—parallel to being hated by people for the Son of Man's sake.
Jesus predicts that disciples will be expelled from synagogues, which corresponds to ἀφορίσωσιν (to be excluded/cast out) in Luke 6:22.
The apostles left the Council rejoicing because they had been counted worthy to suffer dishonor for Jesus' name's sake—an fulfillment of the beatitude about rejoicing in persecution.
Peter says that they are blessed if they are mocked for Christ's name's sake, a direct parallel to being scorned and rejected for the Son of Man's sake.
James encourages counting it pure joy when one meets trials of many kinds, which reflects the call to rejoice in persecution.
John says that believers should not be surprised if the world hates them, confirming that hatred from people is an expected part of following Christ.
